blocks.text: Dear Thomas:

Thank you for the conversations that brought us to this letter, and for the candor with which you and your colleagues described the business unit the company has decided to sell, which we refer to below simply as the Business. This letter sets out the work we will do for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} in preparing the Business for sale and in running the process that sells it, together with the terms on which we will do that work.

A carve-out asks more of a seller than the sale of a whole company does, because buyers are being asked to value something that has never stood on its own, and their first questions will be about what it costs to run the Business without the company around it. Most of what we propose is aimed at answering those questions ourselves, in writing, before the first buyer is called. The deliverables are these, in roughly the order we expect to produce them:

items: A separation profile of the Business, prepared with your finance and operations staff, identifying what it shares with the rest of the company today (people, systems, facilities, and contracts) and what a buyer would need in place on its first day of ownership.

A standalone financial presentation, built with you and your team, that shows the corporate costs now allocated to the Business, our estimate of what those functions would cost a new owner, and the adjustments we expect buyers to raise first.
An outline of the transition services the company would be prepared to provide after closing, and for how long, so that the question is settled on our side before any buyer puts it to us.

A short anonymous profile and a confidential information memorandum, each describing the Business by sector and size, and neither identifying the company to a reader who has not signed a confidentiality agreement you have approved.
A list of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.scope}}, strategic and financial, which we will review with you name by name before anyone is approached, followed by outreach to the parties you approve.

Management of the process from first contact through final bids: confidentiality agreements, the data room, management meetings, the collection and comparison of indications of interest, and our advice on the terms of whichever proposal you choose to pursue.

blocks.text: Some decisions in a carve-out belong to the company alone, chiefly which people, contracts, and systems go with the Business and how long the company will support it after closing. We will put each of them to you as soon as the separation profile shows it to be needed, together with our view of how buyers are likely to read the answer.

Mark Allen, a Partner of the firm, will lead the engagement day to day and will be your first call on any question, however small it seems. Sarah Fletcher, an Advisory Associate, will run buyer outreach and will be the voice most buyers hear from us, while Angela Cole, an Analyst, will build the buyer list and work alongside your team on the standalone financial presentation.

I will stay close to the work throughout, and I will read anything that goes to a buyer under our name before it is sent. We have kept the team small on purpose, so that the people who learn the Business in the first weeks are the same people who explain it to buyers later, and on your side we will look to you as our principal contact unless you tell us otherwise.

We expect the process to run roughly six months, and we will bring a proposed working calendar to our first session with your team. We cannot promise that it will end with a buyer at a price the company is willing to accept, and nothing in this letter should be read as that promise. What we will do is tell you plainly, at each stage, where every party stands.
Fees and payment

Our fee for the engagement described in this letter is {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}. We will invoice it in installments as the work proceeds, and each invoice is payable within thirty days of receipt. Reasonable out-of-pocket expenses, chiefly travel and the cost of the data room, are billed at cost in addition to the fee, and we will ask you before incurring any single expense of real size.
Term and termination

Our work begins on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}} and continues until a transaction closes or one of us brings the engagement to an end. Either of us may end it at any time by written notice to the other; fees invoiced and expenses incurred up to the date of that notice remain payable, and the confidentiality and liability provisions below survive it.
Confidentiality

We will hold in confidence everything the company shares with us and use it only for this engagement. In any material that circulates beyond our two firms, the Business will be described by sector and revenue band rather than by name, and we will disclose the company's identity only to parties that have signed a confidentiality agreement in a form you have approved.
Information and reliance

The company will give us access to the people and records we reasonably need, and will tell us promptly if anything it has given us proves inaccurate or incomplete. We will rely on that information without verifying it independently, and we will say so in any material we prepare from it.
Limitation of liability

Our aggregate liability to the company in connection with this engagement is limited to the fees we have received under this letter, except to the extent a loss is finally determined to have resulted from our gross negligence or willful misconduct. Neither of us will be liable to the other for indirect, special, or consequential damages, however they arise.
Governing law

This letter is governed by the laws of the state in which our principal office is located, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules. It is the whole of our agreement about this engagement, and it may be changed only in a writing that both of us have signed.

If this letter reflects your understanding, please sign both copies where indicated below and return one to me; the other is for your files. When we have it, Mark Allen will call you to set the date of our first working session with your team.

To: Mark Allen, Sarah Fletcher
From: Angela Cole
Re: {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}, carve-out advisory, kickoff
The situation as we understand it

Our engagement with {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} began on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}. The company intends to sell a business unit that has always operated inside it, and what we know about that unit comes from two places: our conversations with Thomas Le, and the first package of management accounts his team sent over. I have kept the two sources apart below, because they will not always agree.

On the accounts, the unit carries an allocation of corporate cost for finance, human resources, information technology, and purchasing, and the allocation appears to be set as a share of revenue rather than built up from use. That is my reading of the schedules; Thomas Le has not yet confirmed it. On the conversations, we were told that the unit runs on the company's own ERP instance, that some of its customer contracts sit with the parent entity rather than with the unit, and that the company has not decided which of the unit's managers would transfer with it. None of those points has been checked.
How we propose to approach it

A buyer will be valuing something that has never had to pay for its own back office, and that fact, more than the unit's growth or its margins, is what will set the tone of the bids. It follows that the first piece of work is the standalone cost picture: what the allocated functions would cost a new owner, which of them a strategic buyer could absorb into its own operations, and which a financial sponsor would have to build or buy. It also follows that the company has to answer the transition services question before we go to market, since a sponsor in particular cannot bid with confidence until it knows how long the ERP and the shared contracts will be supported after closing.

The engagement letter provides for outreach to {{fact:f:E-2019-001.scope}}, and a draft of that list exists. I would hold it back from Thomas Le until the standalone numbers are at least in draft, because the balance between strategic and financial names on it should reflect what those numbers show: if standing the unit up alone is expensive, the strategic names, which can avoid most of that expense, deserve to be called first and given more time. Sarah Fletcher will run the calls in either case, and the anonymous profile she works from should describe the unit by sector and revenue band only. That matters more than usual here, since the parent's identity is the easiest thing in the profile to guess.
The first two weeks

This week I will send Thomas Le a data request covering cost allocations by function, headcount by function and location, the contracts the parent holds on the unit's behalf, and a map of the systems the unit shares. Next week I would like two days with his finance team on the allocations themselves, working from their schedules rather than ours, so that the standalone estimate starts from figures they recognize. In parallel, Sarah Fletcher will draft the anonymous profile and the talking points for her first calls, and Mark Allen will propose the working calendar to Thomas Le at our first session with his team, by which point I will have the buyer list in a form fit to show him, with the basis for each name recorded beside it.
Everything above waits on the data request. I have circulated the draft, and I need Mark Allen's comments on it by tomorrow morning so that it reaches Thomas Le before the end of the week.

blocks.text: Reading the Figures

The buyer list is broad by design, and it should not be read as a forecast of interest. It holds strategic parties that could fold most of the shared functions into their own operations, and financial sponsors that would need the full transition package; Sarah Fletcher's first calls are under way, and we will report the count of parties contacted when the round closes. The precedent set is narrower than we would like, because many sellers do not disclose transition terms, and we would not draw a valuation conclusion from it. With that caveat, it does show that the separations drawing the most interest had settled the length of their transition services before marketing began. Taken together with the standalone cost work, which so far points to information technology as the function a buyer would find hardest to replace, the figures argue for giving every party the transition outline with the memorandum, not after it.
Before Our Next Briefing

items: Sarah Fletcher completes the first-round calls and reports which parties have asked for the memorandum.
Confidentiality agreements go out in the form Thomas Le approved; the memorandum follows only on signature.
Angela Cole closes the open items in the standalone cost estimate with the finance team, marking any figure that remains an estimate.
Mark Allen proposes the date by which indications of interest will be requested.
Thomas Le confirms the transition services period the company is prepared to offer, without which the memorandum cannot be finalized.

blocks.text: Working Session Minutes: {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} Carve-Out

items: Mark Allen, Partner, Quillon Harbor
Angela Cole, Analyst, Quillon Harbor
Sarah Fletcher, Advisory Associate, Quillon Harbor
Michael Duffy, Analyst, Quillon Harbor
Thomas Le, VP Finance, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

blocks.text: The session, in the order taken
First-round outreach is complete and the process is on the calendar agreed with Thomas Le. The open questions are now about the Business, not about buyer interest.

Sarah Fletcher opened with outreach. The first round closed with {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-buyers-contacted}}. She described the response as steady rather than eager: strategic parties asked mostly about customer contracts, and sponsors asked mostly about the transition period. Confidentiality agreements are out with the parties that asked for the memorandum, and several sponsors have objected to the employee non-solicitation clause as drafted. She expects most of the outstanding agreements to be signed within two weeks if the clause is settled.

Michael Duffy reported on his sessions with the company's controller. Allocations for finance, human resources, and purchasing are close to what those functions would cost a new owner. Information technology is the exception: the allocation understates what a buyer would pay to replace it, chiefly because the Business uses the company's ERP instance and licenses at no charge today. His working figure is an estimate and has not yet been reviewed by Thomas Le.

Angela Cole reported on the memorandum and the data room. The memorandum is going to signing parties with the transition section describing services in general terms and the ERP period left open. The data room index follows the separation profile, so that a buyer finds everything the Business shares with the company in one place. She asked that nothing from the controller sessions go into the room until Thomas Le has reviewed Michael Duffy's figures. Agreed.

Thomas Le raised whether to add parties to the list now that the first round is done. Discussed and dropped: the list was approved before outreach, and new names approached now would trail the others by several weeks. Mark Allen raised whether the company should commission a quality-of-earnings review from an outside accounting firm before indications are requested. Thomas Le preferred to wait for buyer feedback, and the point was dropped for this session. Thomas Le also asked when indications would be requested. Mark Allen's answer was that the date follows the ERP decision and should not be fixed before it.
Left open

Three items remain unresolved. The length of ERP transition support sits with Thomas Le, to take to the company's leadership; buyers will price it, and the instruction letter for indications should not go out without it. The customer contracts held by the parent entity rather than by the Business also sit with Thomas Le, working with the company's legal team to establish which of them need counterparty consent to assign. The non-solicitation clause sits with Sarah Fletcher: Mark Allen recommended narrowing it to employees a buyer meets during the process, and she will put that position to the sponsors who objected.
Next session to be set once Thomas Le has the company's answer on ERP support.
Status Report: The Confidentiality Agreement Period
Prepared for Thomas Le, VP Finance, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}, by Angela Cole, Analyst, with Mark Allen and Sarah Fletcher.
Progress against the plan

The process is where the working calendar placed it for this point, with one exception, which is the first risk listed below. First-round outreach closed with {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-buyers-contacted}}, as reported at the last working session, and the period since has been taken up with confidentiality agreements and the first weeks of the data room.

The confidentiality agreement round has produced {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-ndas-executed}} to date, and each signing party has received the memorandum and access to the data room. Sarah Fletcher reports that the sponsors who objected to the non-solicitation clause accepted the narrowed version Mark Allen proposed, and that none withdrew over it. That account comes from her calls; not every party has yet confirmed it in writing.

Data room activity has been steady. Most signed parties opened the room within days of receiving access, and the questions log so far runs to customer contracts, the ERP, and headcount by function, in roughly that order of frequency. The ordering is my reading of the log, not a tally I would stand behind until the log is closed.

The standalone cost bridge has been reviewed with your team for the finance, human resources, and purchasing functions, where the allocated and standalone figures are close. Information technology remains the exception. Our estimate of what a buyer would pay to replace the Business's systems sits well above the current allocation, and it stays an estimate until your team has been through it; it has not been placed in the data room.

Neither of the reference sets has changed. The approved list remains {{fact:f:E-2019-001.scope}}, as you reviewed it, and we continue to read buyer feedback against {{fact:f:E-2019-001.comparators}}. Nothing we have heard so far sits outside what those precedents suggest about how buyers price an unsettled transition period. This is a qualitative reading, since few of the precedents disclose valuation in enough detail to support a numerical one.
Our work remains within the engagement budget set in the letter, a fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}, and the only expense of note has been the data room.
The next stage in the plan is the instruction letter asking signed parties for indications of interest. It is drafted, and it is the item held up by the first risk below.

Once indications are in, we will recommend which parties to invite to management meetings, and we would like the unit's managers to rehearse once with Mark Allen and Sarah Fletcher beforehand. The company's decision on which managers transfer with the Business will be needed by then, since buyers will ask whom they are meeting and whether those people come with the sale.
Open risks

items: ERP transition support. Owner: Thomas Le. Trigger: the instruction letter is ready to go out and the company has not fixed the period of ERP support it will offer. Parties would then bid against different assumptions, and their indications could not be compared on equal terms.

Customer contracts held by the parent entity. Owner: Thomas Le, with the company's legal team. Trigger: any contract that needs counterparty consent to assign and for which consent has not been requested before indications arrive.

Standalone information technology cost. Owner: Angela Cole. Trigger: a buyer's diligence producing a replacement cost for the Business's systems materially above ours, which is still an estimate and has not yet been reviewed by your team.

Sponsor engagement. Owner: Sarah Fletcher. Trigger: a signed party that has not opened the data room within a week of receiving access, which is usually the first sign of a party drifting out of a process.
Confidentiality. Owner: Mark Allen. Trigger: any sign that the company's identity has been discussed with a party that has not signed.

blocks.text: What has changed since the last report

Against the risk list reviewed at the last working session, one risk has closed, one has grown, and one is new. The non-solicitation objection has closed with the narrowed clause. The customer contract question has grown: the company's legal team has identified contracts that appear to need consent to assign, and while the final list is theirs to confirm, the issue is no longer a theoretical one. The standalone technology cost is new to the list, following the controller sessions, and it should be read alongside the ERP risk rather than apart from it, since a longer period of ERP support would reduce what a buyer has to replace on its first day.

The ERP period remains the single decision that most affects the next stage. We would ask for the company's position on it before the instruction letter goes out, and Mark Allen will call you this week to take it.
Working Session Minutes: {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} Carve-Out, Final Round

items: Mark Allen, Partner, Quillon Harbor
Angela Cole, Analyst, Quillon Harbor
Sarah Fletcher, Advisory Associate, Quillon Harbor
Thomas Le, VP Finance, {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}

blocks.text: Decisions

The session reached four decisions. Final proposals will be accepted only against the transition services term sheet as issued, with ERP support for the period stated there and no longer. The proposal deadline will not be extended for any party. A late approach from a party outside the process will be declined. Proposals will be compared on certainty of closing, including financing and customer consents, alongside price.
Discussion

Sarah Fletcher opened by restating the process record, at Thomas Le's request, for the company's leadership. First-round outreach closed with {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-buyers-contacted}}. The confidentiality round produced {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-ndas-executed}}. The indication stage closed with {{fact:f:E-2019-001.pipeline-indications-received}}. Management meetings with the parties selected after the indication stage are complete, and the parties remaining have the draft purchase agreement and the term sheet.

Angela Cole then summarized the indications. They differed more in structure than in headline value. Some assumed the term sheet as drafted; others proposed a longer ERP period, or a price adjustment tied to one; and the sponsors tended to condition their figures on customer consents being in hand before signing. Her view, which Mark Allen shared, was that proposals built on different assumptions cannot be ranked on price alone, and that the final round should remove as many of those differences as the company can.

The term sheet decision came out of the management meetings. Sponsors asked in their sessions whether ERP support could run longer than the term sheet allows. Thomas Le said the company would not extend it, and Mark Allen recommended that the position be confirmed in writing so that no proposal arrives priced on a longer period. The deadline decision was Thomas Le's: the company's leadership is not prepared to reopen the timetable for a slow bidder.

The late approach reached Sarah Fletcher last week from a party that declined to sign a confidentiality agreement in the summer. Angela Cole noted that admitting it now would mean a fresh data room review and a new round of diligence questions, and the meeting agreed that the cost outweighed the chance of a better proposal. The comparison criteria came from Angela Cole's draft framework. She will revise it to show customer consents as their own line, since the company's legal team has now requested every consent it identified and the answers will arrive with the proposals or shortly after.
Actions

items: Sarah Fletcher: write to the remaining parties confirming that the proposal deadline stands and that proposals must follow the term sheet as issued.
Sarah Fletcher: decline the late approach in writing, without confirming the company's identity.
Angela Cole: revise the comparison framework with customer consents shown separately, and circulate it to Thomas Le before proposals arrive.
Thomas Le: confirm the status of each outstanding customer consent with the company's legal team.
Mark Allen: schedule the session at which the proposals will be reviewed with Thomas Le and the company's leadership.
